issues.legal_issue: Government approval of a scheme initiated after an area declaration need not precede the scheme’s initial publication and, once obtained, validates prior steps taken in anticipation of approval.
material_facts: The area was declared before the scheme was notified.
The government approved the scheme after its initial notification but before the later declaration concerning the acquired area.
The statutory exception required government approval but did not expressly require prior approval.
issues.conclusion: Prior government approval was not required. Once approval was obtained, the earlier acts and publications made in anticipation of it were validated.
issues.legal_principle: Under exception (iii) to section 59(1)(a) of the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, approval of the State Government is required for a scheme initiated after an area declaration, but the provision does not require that approval to be obtained beforehand. The distinction between approval and permission, and whether prior approval should be implied, depends on the statutory language and context. The Court relied on Life Insurance Corpn. of India v. Escorts Ltd. (1986) 1 SCC 264 and Lord Krishna Textiles Mills Ltd. v. Workmen, 1961 (1) L.L.J. 211, and held that subsequent approval validates acts previously taken in anticipation of it.

rule.if: statutory_scheme_validity_case and scheme_initiated_after_area_declaration and initial_publication_preceded_approval and government_approved_scheme

predicates.statutory_scheme_validity_case: The proceeding concerns whether steps taken to implement a statutory scheme are valid.
predicates.scheme_initiated_after_area_declaration: The scheme was initiated after the relevant area had been declared for development.
predicates.initial_publication_preceded_approval: The scheme was initially published before government approval was obtained.
predicates.government_approved_scheme: The government later approved the scheme.

issues.definition: When a statutory scheme validity proceeding concerns a scheme initiated after an area declaration, and the scheme was initially published before the government later approved it, the earlier steps are validated.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal warrants no interference where the appellant has compromised with other similarly situated claimants but has not extended the same treatment to respondents who need housing sites.
material_facts: The appellant had compromised with others in similar circumstances but had not extended that compromise to the respondents.
The respondents’ society included members who needed sites to construct homes.
The appeal was before the Court by special leave.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere and dismissed the appeal, while declaring the law on the approval issue.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined discretionary interference under Article 136 in light of the appellant’s compromise with other similarly situated persons and its failure to extend that treatment to the respondents. It also relied on the principle that the right to shelter is a fundamental right deriving from the rights to residence under Article 19(1)(e) and to life under Article 21. Construction must comply with applicable layout and building rules, but that is not by itself a reason to refuse permission when permission is sought in accordance with law.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and compromise_extended_to_similar_claimants and compromise_not_extended_to_respondents and respondents_need_housing_sites

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.compromise_extended_to_similar_claimants: The appellant had compromised with other claimants in similar circumstances.
predicates.compromise_not_extended_to_respondents: The appellant had not extended the same compromise to the respondents.
predicates.respondents_need_housing_sites: The respondents included people who needed sites to build homes.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, when the appellant has compromised with similar claimants but not the respondents, who need housing sites, the appeal is dismissed without interference.
